sections.b: The first six chapters introduce the prophet and his message before the story of his call. Chapter 1 is a summary of the whole book: the LORD's lawsuit against his rebellious children, worship rejected for lack of justice, an offer of cleansing and the promise of a refined Zion. Chapters 2–4 set the nations streaming to Zion to learn God's ways (2:2–4) against the day of the LORD on all human pride (2:6–22), the collapse of Jerusalem's leadership (3) and a purified remnant (4:2–6). Chapter 5 sings the song of the vineyard and pronounces six woes. Only then, in chapter 6, does Isaiah tell of the year King Uzziah died, when he saw the Lord on his throne and heard the seraphim cry 'Holy, holy, holy'. From that vision comes his name for God, 'the Holy One of Israel', and his hardest commission.
sections.refs: Isaiah 1:1–31; Isaiah 2:1–4; Isaiah 5:1–7; Isaiah 6:1–13

common: Isaiah's call to be a prophet is told in chapter 6, not at the start of the book.
uncommon: Some scholars hold that chapter 6 is not Isaiah's first call but a later commission for a new task.

sections.b: Isaiah's vision gave the Bible its most famous words about holiness: the seraphim cry 'Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies' (Isaiah 6:3), the threefold form of the Hebrew superlative. Holiness here is not only moral purity but God's majesty, before which even the seraphim cover their faces and a human being cries 'Woe to me!' (6:5). Yet the holy God is also 'the Holy One of Israel', Isaiah's favorite name for him (1:4; 5:19, 24), bound to a sinful people. Isaiah links holiness with justice: 'the holy God proves that he is holy' through righteousness (5:16). The survivors who are cleansed will themselves be 'called holy' (4:3), and the stump left after judgment is 'a holy seed' (6:13). The seraphim's song became the Jewish Kedushah and the Christian Sanctus, and is sung in heaven in Revelation 4:8.
sections.refs: Isaiah 6:1–7; Isaiah 1:4; Isaiah 4:3; Isaiah 5:16; Isaiah 6:13; Revelation 4:8; Leviticus 19:2

common: The seraphim's 'Holy, holy, holy' is sung every week in Christian and Jewish worship.

sections.h: The mountain of the LORD's house (Isaiah 2:2–4)
sections.b: Zion was a modest hill, lower than the Mount of Olives across the valley. Isaiah sees it 'set firm at the head of the mountains' in the days to come, with all the nations streaming to it like a river running uphill (Isaiah 2:2). They come not to conquer but to learn: 'from Zion comes teaching, and from Jerusalem, the LORD's word' (2:3). The same oracle stands in Micah 4:1–3. Isaiah 4:5–6 adds a second picture: the cloud and fire of the wilderness resting over the whole of Mount Zion as a canopy and shelter. Psalms 46 and 48 praise Zion as the city of God; Isaiah makes it the center of a world at peace. Hebrews 12:22 says believers 'have come to Mount Zion', and Revelation's new Jerusalem draws on the same hope.
sections.refs: Isaiah 2:2–4; Isaiah 4:5–6; Micah 4:1–3; Psalm 48:1–2; Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:10

common: Isaiah 2:2–4 and Micah 4:1–3 are the same oracle.

sections.b: The first chapters of Isaiah build the idea of a remnant step by step. After invasion, 'a handful of us' is all that keeps Jerusalem from Sodom's fate (Isaiah 1:9), and Paul quotes the verse in the Greek's form, 'a seed', for the believing remnant of Israel (Romans 9:29). Zion will be refined like silver, its dross burned away (1:25–27). The survivors left in Jerusalem will be called holy and written down for life (4:2–3). The call vision ends with the harshest picture: even the tenth left will be burned again, like a felled tree, yet 'its stump is a holy seed' (6:13). The name of Isaiah's son, Shear-jashub, 'a remnant will turn back' (7:3), gathers these threads. The remnant is not the righteous who escape on their own merit, but what God's judgment leaves and his mercy keeps.
sections.refs: Isaiah 1:9; Isaiah 1:25–27; Isaiah 4:2–4; Isaiah 6:13; Isaiah 7:3; Romans 9:27–29; Romans 11:5

sections.h: The day against all that is proud (Isaiah 2:6–22)
sections.b: Isaiah 2:12–22 is the first long poem on the day of the LORD, which Amos had already turned from a hope into a threat (Amos 5:18–20). The day is 'set against all that is proud and towering': the cedars of Lebanon and the oaks of Bashan, mountains and hills, towers and walls, the great ships of Tarshish (Isaiah 2:12–16). A refrain gives the point: 'the LORD alone will stand high on that day' (2:11, 17). People throw their idols to the moles and bats and hide in caves 'away from the dread of the LORD and his majestic splendor' (2:19–21), a scene Revelation 6:15–16 takes up. Isaiah 5:30 ends the first chapters in darkness. Later prophets and the New Testament carry the image forward to the final judgment.
sections.refs: Isaiah 2:6–22; Isaiah 5:30; Amos 5:18–20; Zephaniah 1:14–18; Revelation 6:15–16

sections.b: Isaiah's song is the fullest picture of Israel as God's vineyard. The owner picks a fertile hill, clears its stones, plants the choicest vines, builds a tower and cuts a wine vat, and the vines give 'stinking grapes' (Isaiah 5:1–2). He asks the hearers to judge, then tears down the hedge and forbids the rain (5:3–6). Only at the end is the vineyard named: 'the house of Israel', which yielded bloodshed instead of justice (5:7). Isaiah 3:14 had already accused the leaders of grazing it bare, and 27:2–6 sings a new song of a vineyard the LORD guards night and day. Psalm 80 and Jeremiah 2:21 use the same image. Jesus' parable of the tenants begins with Isaiah's words (Mark 12:1), and in John 15 Jesus calls himself the true vine.
sections.refs: Isaiah 5:1–7; Isaiah 3:14; Isaiah 27:2–6; Psalm 80:8–16; Jeremiah 2:21; Mark 12:1–12; John 15:1–8

sections.h: A parable that traps its hearers (Isaiah 5:1–7)
sections.b: The song of the vineyard works as a juridical parable, like Nathan's story of the poor man's lamb (2 Samuel 12:1–7) or the prophet's trap for Ahab (1 Kings 20:39–42). The people of Jerusalem are asked to judge a case about a vineyard, and agree that the owner did everything he could (Isaiah 5:3–4). Only then are they told that the vineyard is themselves (5:7). Gale Yee showed how closely the song follows the form of such legal parables. Jesus told his parable of the tenants with the same vineyard and the same kind of trap, so that the chief priests 'knew he had spoken the parable against them' (Mark 12:12).
sections.refs: Isaiah 5:1–7; 2 Samuel 12:1–7; 1 Kings 20:39–42; Mark 12:1–12; Matthew 21:33–46

sections.b: 'I saw the Lord', Isaiah says (Isaiah 6:1), and later, 'with my own eyes I have seen the King' (6:5). He fears for his life, as one who knew that "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20). Yet he describes almost nothing of God himself: only a throne, the hem of a robe that fills the Temple, and the seraphim who hide their faces. The Targum says he saw 'the glory of the LORD'. The Talmud tells that King Manasseh used the verse to accuse Isaiah of contradicting Moses before he had him killed (Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 49b). John says Isaiah 'had seen his glory', meaning Christ's (John 12:41), and many church fathers held that the one seen was the Son.
sections.refs: Isaiah 6:1–5; Exodus 33:20; 1 Kings 22:19; Ezekiel 1:26–28; John 12:41; John 1:18

sections.b: The seraphim appear in the Bible only in Isaiah 6. Their name means 'burning ones', the word used for the 'burning snakes' of the wilderness (Numbers 21:6) and for the 'flying seraph' of Isaiah 14:29 and 30:6. Judean seals of the 700s BC show winged cobras, and many scholars think Isaiah pictured the seraphim as fiery winged serpents. In the vision they have six wings, faces, feet, hands and voices; they hover above the throne, cover their faces, sing 'Holy, holy, holy' and carry a hot stone from the altar to cleanse Isaiah's lips. Later Jewish and Christian tradition ranked them highest among the angels (Pseudo-Dionysius, The Celestial Hierarchy), and the living creatures of Revelation 4:8 sing their song.
sections.refs: Isaiah 6:2–7; Isaiah 14:29; Isaiah 30:6; Numbers 21:6–9; Revelation 4:8; Ezekiel 1:5–11

sections.b: In Isaiah's vision the Lord asks, 'Whom am I to send? Who will go for us?' (Isaiah 6:8). Most scholars hear the plural as God speaking to his heavenly court, as in Micaiah's vision, where the LORD sits on his throne 'and all the army of heaven' stands beside him and he asks who will go (1 Kings 22:19–22). Isaiah, a human being, steps into the council and volunteers. Other readers explain the 'us' as a plural of deliberation, and many church fathers heard in it the Trinity, linked with the threefold 'holy' of 6:3.
sections.refs: Isaiah 6:1–8; 1 Kings 22:19–22; Genesis 1:26; Job 1:6; Psalm 82:1; Jeremiah 23:18

sections.b: Isaiah's commission is to tell the people to listen and not understand, and to 'make this people's heart fat ... or else they may ... turn back, and be healed' (Isaiah 6:9–10). The Greek turns the commands into a description, 'this people's heart has grown fat', and Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27 quote the Greek. Mark 4:12 ends 'and be forgiven', as the Targum does. John 12:40 makes God the one who blinds. Readers explain the passage as a result stated as if it were a purpose, as judicial hardening after long refusal, or as a hardening limited in time: 'until' the judgment (6:11), with a holy seed left (6:13). Paul says Israel's hardening is partial and lasts until the full number of the Gentiles comes in (Romans 11:25).
sections.refs: Isaiah 6:9–13; Matthew 13:13–15; Mark 4:11–12; Luke 8:10; John 12:39–41; Acts 28:25–28; Romans 11:7–10; Romans 11:25

sections.b: Isaiah uses Sodom and Gomorrah three ways in his opening chapters. They are what Jerusalem would have become without a handful of survivors (Isaiah 1:9). They are what Jerusalem already is: 'you rulers of Sodom! ... you people of Gomorrah!' (1:10). And Jerusalem's sin is as open as theirs: 'They announce their sin as Sodom did and make no effort to cover it' (3:9). The 'outcry' God hears from the vineyard (5:7) is the word for the outcry against Sodom (Genesis 18:20). Isaiah names Sodom's sin in terms of injustice, bloodshed and bribery, as Ezekiel 16:49 does in terms of pride and neglect of the poor.
sections.refs: Isaiah 1:9–10; Isaiah 3:9; Isaiah 5:7; Genesis 18:20–21; Genesis 19:24–25; Ezekiel 16:49; Romans 9:29

sections.b: Isaiah's book is dated by kings, beginning with Uzziah (Isaiah 1:1), and his vision 'in the year King Uzziah died', about 740 BC (6:1). Chronicles tells that Uzziah, proud of his power, went into the Temple to burn incense, which only priests could do, and was struck with a skin disease; he lived in isolation until his death (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Isaiah's vision takes place in that same Temple, full of smoke, before the true King. Many readers have seen the contrast as deliberate: the king who forced his way into God's presence is gone, and the prophet who is undone by it is cleansed and sent. Chronicles also says that Isaiah wrote 'the rest of the acts of Uzziah' (2 Chronicles 26:22).
sections.refs: Isaiah 1:1; Isaiah 6:1–5; 2 Chronicles 26:16–23; 2 Kings 15:1–7

sections.b: The pair mishpat and tsedaqah, justice and righteousness, runs through Isaiah's opening chapters. Jerusalem 'was filled with justice' and righteousness once 'stayed the night in her' (Isaiah 1:21); now its officials take bribes and ignore the orphan and widow (1:23). Worship cannot replace it: 'Go after justice. ... Give the orphan his rights; take up the widow's case' (1:17). Zion will be ransomed through justice and righteousness (1:27). The vineyard song ends with Isaiah's most famous wordplay: God waited for mishpat and got mishpach, bloodshed; for tsedaqah and heard tse'aqah, an outcry (5:7). Even God's holiness is shown through justice (5:16). Amos 5:24 and Micah 6:8 make the same demand.
sections.refs: Isaiah 1:17; Isaiah 1:21–27; Isaiah 5:7; Isaiah 5:16; Isaiah 5:23; Amos 5:24; Micah 6:8

sections.b: The Hebrew be'acharit hayyamim, 'at the end of the days', opens Isaiah's vision of the nations coming to Zion (Isaiah 2:2; Micah 4:1). The phrase can mean simply 'in the future' (Genesis 49:1), but here it introduces a future unlike the present: the LORD's mountain highest of all, the nations taught by him, and war unlearned (2:2–4). Jewish tradition reads it of the days of the Messiah. The New Testament says the last days began with Jesus and the gift of the Spirit (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), and Christians differ over how much of Isaiah 2:2–4 is being kept now and how much waits for Christ's return.
sections.refs: Isaiah 2:2–4; Micah 4:1–3; Genesis 49:1; Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2

sections.b: 'They will pound their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning knives' (Isaiah 2:4) is the Bible's best-known picture of disarmament. The peace comes after the nations learn the LORD's ways and he judges their disputes (2:3–4). Justin Martyr claimed it was being fulfilled as Christians, once violent, became peaceable (First Apology 39). Peace churches read it as a call to refuse war now; just war traditions read it as the goal of the kingdom, not a law for governments in this age; dispensationalists place it in Christ's coming reign on earth. Joel 3:10 reverses the image in a call to battle. A statue on the theme by Evgeny Vuchetich has stood at the United Nations in New York since 1959.
sections.refs: Isaiah 2:2–4; Micah 4:3–4; Joel 3:10; Matthew 5:9; Matthew 26:52

sections.b: 'On that day the LORD's branch will become a thing of beauty and glory' (Isaiah 4:2). The Targum reads 'the Messiah of the LORD', and many Christian readers have followed, linking the verse with Jeremiah's 'righteous branch' for David (Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15) and Zechariah's 'Branch' (Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12). Most modern commentators read it as the land's new growth after devastation, since the next line speaks of 'the fruit of the land'; the Greek has no branch at all. Isaiah's clearest pictures of the coming king come later, in 9:6–7 and 11:1–10.
sections.refs: Isaiah 4:2; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5; Jeremiah 33:15; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12

sections.b: The survivors in Jerusalem will be 'called holy: everyone in Jerusalem whose name is written down for life' (Isaiah 4:3). The image comes from a city's register of its living citizens (Nehemiah 7:5), but it points to God's own book, from which Moses asked to be wiped out (Exodus 32:32) and from which a psalm asks that the wicked be removed (Psalm 69:28). Daniel 12:1 and Revelation 20:12–15 and 21:27 develop it into the book of those who will share the life to come.
sections.refs: Isaiah 4:3; Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1; Malachi 3:16; Revelation 20:12–15; Revelation 21:27

sections.b: Isaiah 4:5 promises that the LORD will 'create' over Mount Zion 'a cloud in the daytime and smoke, and at night the bright light of a blazing fire', the signs that led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 13:21–22) and filled the tabernacle and Temple (Exodus 40:34–38; 1 Kings 8:10–11). Now they rest over every place and every gathering on Zion, as a canopy and a booth against heat and storm (Isaiah 4:6). It is one of the first hints in the book of a new exodus, a theme that grows in chapters 11, 35 and 40–55.
sections.refs: Isaiah 4:5–6; Exodus 13:21–22; Exodus 40:34–38; 1 Kings 8:10–11; Isaiah 11:15–16; Isaiah 52:12

sections.h: Woe to those who string house onto house (Isaiah 5:8–10)
sections.b: The first woe of Isaiah 5 is against land-grabbers: 'those who string house onto house and attach field to field until no space remains' (Isaiah 5:8). Israel's law treated land as the LORD's, held by families who could not sell it for good (Leviticus 25:23); Naboth would not sell his vineyard even to the king (1 Kings 21:3). In the wealth of the 700s, Micah and Isaiah saw small farms swallowed into estates (Micah 2:1–2). Isaiah's sentence fits the crime: the great houses will stand empty, and ten acres of vines will give six gallons of wine (Isaiah 5:9–10). The women's finery of 3:18–23 is the same wealth seen from inside the house: 'what you stole from the poor' (3:14).
sections.refs: Isaiah 5:8–10; Isaiah 3:14–23; Leviticus 25:23; 1 Kings 21:1–3; Micah 2:1–2; Amos 6:4–7

sections.b: In Isaiah 5:14 Sheol, the world of the dead, opens its throat wide and swallows Jerusalem's nobles and crowds. The picture of death as a monstrous mouth is old: in the Ugaritic Baal poems, the god Mot ('Death') has one lip to the earth and one to the heavens. Proverbs 30:15–16 and Habakkuk 2:5 also speak of Sheol's endless appetite. Isaiah later reverses it: the LORD 'will swallow up death forever' (Isaiah 25:8), the verse Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 15:54.
sections.refs: Isaiah 5:14; Isaiah 25:8; Proverbs 27:20; Proverbs 30:15–16; Habakkuk 2:5; 1 Corinthians 15:54
